items: So cost can differ per user and change over time
Always compare with the library verify/compare
Never hash(input) === stored on raw digests: that leaks timing

blocks.title: Acceptable Fallbacks
items: scrypt is fine
PBKDF2 when FIPS forces it, >=600k iterations for SHA-256
argon2id stays the default choice
One generic message: 'invalid email or password'
Match the timing too: hash a dummy password when no user exists
Side doors leak the same fact: signup 'email already taken'
So do password reset copy and differing HTTP status codes
Per-account limits stop targeted brute force
Per-IP and per-ASN limits stop credential stuffing
Stuffing is the dominant real attack: replayed breach pairs
Check candidates against a breach corpus, k-anonymity on the SHA-1 prefix

blocks.title: Policy That Actually Works
items: Minimum 8-12 chars, allow 64+ and full Unicode
Block breached and trivially weak passwords
Drop forced periodic rotation (NIST SP 800-63B)
Normalize NFKC before hashing, never lowercase or strip

lines: }  // the only way to upgrade old users

items: Single-use and high-entropy
15-60 minute expiry, no longer
Stored hashed server-side, like a password
Invalidated on use and on any password change
On password change, kill all other sessions and refresh tokens
Otherwise an attacker who is already in simply stays in
Compare secrets with crypto.timingSafeEqual on fixed-length digests
Length differences still leak, so hash before comparing
Re-ask for the password or a second factor on high-risk actions
Email change, MFA disable, adding a payout account
An active session is not enough authority for those

blocks.title: MFA Storage Details
items: TOTP secrets encrypted at rest
Recovery codes hashed like passwords, single-use
Reject a reused TOTP code inside its window
Rotation is the general defense against undetected compromise
Short life plus regular replacement shrinks the useful window
Access token: short, 5-15 min, carries claims
Refresh token: long, days to months, opaque and server-stored
Every refresh issues a new token and burns the old one
So any given refresh token is single-use
A consumed token presented again means it was stolen and replayed
Revoke the entire token family and force re-authentication

caption.text: Part 3 of WEB AUTH HANDBOOK. Most auth bugs are not exotic crypto failures, they are a missing cookie flag, an unpinned algorithm, or a token parked in localStorage for 30 days. This handbook walks the whole wire: sessions vs JWT with real numbers, every cookie attribute that matters, CSRF exploits and their actual defenses, argon2id parameters, and rotation with refresh-token reuse detection. Twelve chapters of dense notes, ending in a cheat sheet you can ship against.
